content: Psychological and educational interventions have been utilized as supplementary approaches to conventional treatments for children with atopic eczema, aiming to improve the effectiveness of topical therapies. This review is an updated version of the original Cochrane review. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of psychological and educational interventions on managing atopic eczema in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted up to January 2013, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, OpenGrey, and PsycINFO. Additionally, six trial registries were searched, and reference lists of included and excluded studies were reviewed to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The selection criteria focused on RCTs that assessed psychological or educational interventions, or both, designed to assist children and their caregivers in managing atopic eczema. Three authors independently applied the eligibility criteria, evaluated the quality of the trials, and extracted data. However, due to the lack of comparable data, a meta-analysis could not be performed. A total of 10 RCTs were included in this review, five of which were new additions. All interventions were adjuncts to conventional therapy and were delivered in primary and secondary care settings. The studies involved 2003 participants in nine educational interventions and 44 participants in one psychological intervention. Some studies exhibited methodological weaknesses, such as high risks of detection bias, attrition bias, or other biases. The primary outcomes assessed were participant-rated global assessment, reduction in disease severity (measured using the objective SCORAD tool), and improvements in sleep and quality of life. None of the studies reported participant-rated global assessment or sleep improvement. The largest and most robust study, involving 992 participants, demonstrated significant reductions in disease severity and improvements in quality of life in both nurse-led and dermatologist-led intervention groups. This study provided six standardized, age-appropriate group education sessions. Statistically significant improvements in disease severity, as measured by SCORAD, were observed in all intervention groups compared to controls. The improvements in SCORAD scores by age group were as follows: Age 3 months to 7 years: 4.2 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.7 to 6.8) Age 8 to 12 years: 6.7 (95% CI 2.1 to 11.2) Age 13 to 18 years: 9.9 (95% CI 4.3 to 15.5) In three of the five studies that could not be combined due to heterogeneity, the intervention groups showed statistically significant improvements in SCORAD scores compared to usual care groups. However, in all these studies, the confidence interval limits did not exceed the minimum clinically important difference of 8.2 for SCORAD. The largest study also assessed quality of life using the validated German Quality of life in parents of children with atopic dermatitis questionnaire, which includes five subscales. Parents of children under seven years old reported significantly better improvements in the intervention group across all five subscales. For parents of children aged 8 to 12 years, significant improvements were observed in three of the five subscales. This updated review incorporated five new RCTs that used educational interventions as adjuncts to conventional treatments for children with atopic eczema. No additional studies on psychological interventions were identified. The inclusion of these new studies did not significantly alter the conclusions of the original review. The educational studies, both in the original review and this update, lacked detailed descriptions of intervention design and did not employ a complex interventions framework. Few studies used an explicit theoretical basis, and the components of the interventions were not sufficiently described to allow replication. The limited number of rigorously designed trials provides only modest evidence supporting the effectiveness of educational and psychological interventions in managing atopic eczema in children. However, some evidence suggests that certain educational intervention models, such as multiprofessional eczema interventions and nurse-led clinics, may lead to improvements in disease severity and quality of life. Further development of these interventions using a complex interventions framework is necessary. Comparative evaluations are needed to assess their impact on eczema severity, quality of life, psychological distress, and cost-effectiveness. Additionally, future research should compare educational interventions with stand-alone psychosocial self-help approaches.
